The Greek barbel (Luciobarbus graecus) is a potamodromous cyprinid endemic to the Acheloos River basin of western Greece. Females attain sexual maturation at a total length of 17.5 cm [Lp = 17.5 cm], a size that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 72.5 grams [Wwp = 72.5 grams], estimated from length-weight regressions derived for the genus. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], this species exhibits a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of approximately 10% [GSI = approximately 10%]. Field surveys indicate that the species occupies fast-flowing, gravel-bottomed stretches of the river, where ripe individuals congregate during late spring.

Hatchlings of Luciobarbus graecus emerge from demersal, adhesive eggs measuring approximately 1.7 mm in diameter, and the newly hatched prolarvae possess a wet weight at birth of just 0.0026 grams [Wwb = 0.0026 grams]. This minute initial mass, characteristic of cyprinids that produce small, yolk-laden eggs, places the larvae in a high-risk, high-mortality phase immediately following yolk absorption. The exogenous feeding onset occurs when the mouth gape opens and retinal differentiation is sufficient for prey detection, typically a few days after hatching. The prolarvae are lecithotrophic during the earliest days, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves. As the yolk-sac is progressively resorbed, the free-swimming larvae become actively growing, exogenously feeding ichthyoplankton drifting in the river's drift. The transition to the actively foraging pelagic larval stage is a critical bottleneck, with mortality rates strongly influenced by the availability of microcrustaceans and by water temperature, which modulates larval metabolic demands and growth efficiency during this vulnerable period.

As the larvae undergo morphological transformation, the allometric shift marking the larval-juvenile transition is completed as the post-flexion larvae develop fin ray ossification and scale formation. The growing juveniles that recruit to benthic habitats begin to feed on macroinvertebrates and increasingly resemble the adult body plan. Over successive growth seasons, individuals approach their ultimate total length of 50 cm [Li = 50 cm], a maximum size recorded from older specimens in the wild. The corresponding ultimate wet weight, derived from the species-specific length-weight relationship, reaches approximately 1939 grams [Wwi = approximately 1939 grams], a mass that is attained only after several years of sustained feeding on benthic invertebrates and, in larger adults, small fish. Growth rates in this species are known to decelerate markedly after sexual maturity, with energetic resources increasingly channeled into gonadal development rather than somatic growth, a pattern consistent with many temperate freshwater cyprinids displaying asymptotic growth curves.

The maximum documented lifespan for Luciobarbus graecus, as recorded from mark-recapture studies and validated by otolith annuli counts, is 8 years [am = 8 years] when individuals are maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This longevity, while not exceptional among Mediterranean barbels, is noteworthy given the species' relatively slow growth trajectory and the thermal regime of its native habitat. The link between temperature and aging is apparent in this polkilothermic fish; the metabolic rate at 18 °C [T = 18 °C] is sufficiently low to permit an extended reproductive window without the accelerated senescence observed in populations inhabiting warmer lowland reaches. Senescence in the oldest individuals manifests as a decline in condition factor and a gradual reduction in gonado-somatic index during the final year of life. Natural mortality typically occurs during post-spawning periods, when energy stores are most depleted and individuals are vulnerable to environmental stressors.

Females of Luciobarbus graecus produce between 5,000 and 12,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = between 5,000 and 12,000 eggs per spawning event], a fecundity that is moderate for a cyprinid of its size class. Spawning occurs only once per year [F_R_i = Spawning occurs only once per year], usually in May or early June when river temperatures rise above 15 °C. The combination of a single annual reproductive event and a moderate fecundity per event yields an annually modest reproductive output compared to batch-spawning congeners. However, the species compensates for low annual fecundity through extended iteroparity, with females remaining reproductively viable across the full 8-year lifespan (8 years) [am = 8 years] at 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This life history strategy is well-suited to the stable but resource-limited oligotrophic conditions of the Acheloos headwaters, where a high-fecundity, short-lifespan strategy would risk depleting local food resources for larvae.
